question: Your nightly Spark ETL container image is 3.5 GB, and pulling it to autoscaled nodes adds several minutes to every job. How do you reduce the image size and speed up job startup?
directAnswer: Attack the image size with a multi-stage build that leaves build tooling behind, a slim base image, pinned and minimal dependencies, and consolidated RUN layers that clean caches. Then speed up pulls by using a shared base image across jobs so nodes cache common layers, pre-pulling or warming images on nodes, and hosting the registry close to the cluster. Together these typically cut a bloated image to a fraction of its size and slash cold-start pull time.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: This is an image-optimization and startup-latency problem. The container is fat because it carries build tooling, redundant caches, and possibly a heavy base, and every autoscaled node pays to pull the whole thing before the job can run.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Images grow organically: a full base image, apt and pip caches left in layers, build compilers that are only needed at build time, and unpinned dependencies pulling extras. On autoscaled clusters, each new node cold-pulls the image, so the bloat directly becomes startup latency and cost.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: A multi-stage build compiles wheels and native deps in a builder stage and copies only the finished virtual environment into a slim final stage, discarding compilers. Using python:3.11-slim (or distroless) as the runtime base removes hundreds of megabytes. Chaining RUN commands and cleaning apt/pip caches in the same layer avoids persisting caches. Sharing a common base across all job images means nodes cache those layers once, so subsequent pulls only fetch small job-specific layers.

whyImportant: Slow image pulls directly hurt job latency and cost on elastic clusters, and this is a very common real-world pain point when moving data jobs to Kubernetes. Being able to diagnose and fix image bloat systematically is a practical, high-impact skill.
realWorldExample: A team's 3.5 GB Spark image is rebuilt with a multi-stage build on python:3.11-slim: gcc and dev headers stay in the builder, only the venv ships, and apt caches are cleaned inline. The image drops to 800 MB. They also standardize all job images on one Spark base layer, so autoscaled nodes cache it once and new jobs pull only a small delta, cutting cold-start pull time from minutes to seconds.

nestedTopics.title: Multi-stage + slim base
nestedTopics.explanation: The biggest wins come from a multi-stage build that discards build tooling and choosing a minimal runtime base (slim or distroless). This alone often removes over half the size without touching your actual dependencies.

nestedTopics.title: Layer sharing across jobs
nestedTopics.explanation: If all job images share a common base and dependency layer, nodes download those layers once and reuse them for every job image, so only the small top layers transfer per new job. Standardizing bases is a cluster-wide speedup.

nestedTopics.title: Pre-pulling and image warming
nestedTopics.explanation: Techniques like a DaemonSet that pre-pulls critical images onto nodes, node image caching, or keeping a warm node pool ensure the image is already present before a job schedules, removing pull latency from the critical path.

followUps.question: How would you find which part of the image is so large?
followUps.answer: Run docker history <image> to see the size contributed by each layer and instruction, which quickly reveals whether the base, a pip install, or a leftover cache is the culprit. Tools like dive give an interactive, per-layer view and highlight wasted space and duplicated files. Once you know which layer is heavy, you target it, switch to a slimmer base, move a compiler to a builder stage, or clean a cache in the same RUN.

followUps.question: Does using distroless have downsides here?
followUps.answer: Yes: distroless images have no shell or package manager, so you cannot kubectl exec a shell into the container to debug, and installing an ad-hoc tool during an incident is not possible. For Spark specifically you must ensure the required runtime (JRE, Python) is present in the distroless variant you pick. Many teams ship distroless to production for the size and security benefits but keep a debug image variant available for troubleshooting.

followUps.question: If pulls are still slow after optimizing, what else can you do?
followUps.answer: Move the registry closer to the cluster (same region, or a pull-through cache/mirror) to reduce transfer latency, enable registry and node-level image caching, and pre-pull the image onto nodes via a DaemonSet or a warm node pool so it is present before jobs schedule. You can also keep a small buffer of ready nodes so bursts do not require cold node provisioning plus a fresh pull. These address latency that image slimming alone cannot.

question: A teammate manually changed a production S3 bucket policy in the AWS console, and now terraform plan wants to revert it. How do you investigate and resolve this safely?
directAnswer: This is configuration drift: reality diverged from Terraform's state and code. First, do not blindly apply. Run terraform plan to see exactly what would change, then determine whether the manual change was legitimate or a mistake. If it was a needed fix, codify it into the Terraform configuration so plan shows no change; if it was accidental, apply Terraform to restore the intended state. Either way, the resolution ends with git and reality in agreement, and you address why manual changes happened.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Drift occurs when a resource managed by Terraform is modified outside Terraform. Terraform's next plan compares the code and state against the live resource and proposes to overwrite the out-of-band change, which can be destructive if the manual change was actually important.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: People make emergency or convenience changes directly in the console, bypassing the IaC workflow. Terraform, being declarative, treats its configuration as truth and wants to reconcile the drifted resource back to it, so the very next apply threatens to undo the manual change.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: terraform plan refreshes against AWS and shows the diff between the live bucket policy and the coded one. You inspect the diff to understand what changed and why. If the manual change should persist, you update the Terraform code (and possibly import any new sub-resources) so the code matches reality, making the drift disappear from the plan. If it should not persist, you apply to restore the coded policy. Finally, you tighten access or add guardrails so ad-hoc console edits are prevented or detected earlier.

whyImportant: Drift is one of the most common real-world IaC headaches, and mishandling it can cause outages (reverting a critical fix) or silent divergence. Demonstrating a calm, correct process, investigate, decide, codify or restore, then prevent, shows operational maturity.
realWorldExample: An engineer notices terraform plan wants to remove a bucket policy statement that grants a new analytics role read access. They discover a teammate added it manually to unblock a report. Rather than reverting it, they add the statement to the Terraform config, run plan to confirm zero changes, and merge. They then enable drift detection and restrict console write access so future changes go through pull requests.

nestedTopics.title: Investigate before applying
nestedTopics.explanation: Always read the plan carefully and understand the manual change's intent before acting. Blindly applying could revert a legitimate emergency fix and cause an outage; blindly ignoring leaves persistent drift. The decision hinges on whether the manual change was correct.

nestedTopics.title: Codify legitimate changes
nestedTopics.explanation: If the manual change is something you want to keep, the fix is to bring it into code so Terraform's plan becomes a no-op. This may require terraform import for resources created outside Terraform. Now git reflects reality and future applies are safe.

nestedTopics.title: Prevent recurrence
nestedTopics.explanation: Reduce or remove human write access to Terraform-managed resources, run scheduled drift detection (terraform plan in CI) to catch divergence early, and use policy and GitOps so all changes flow through reviewed pull requests.

followUps.question: How can you detect drift proactively instead of stumbling on it?
followUps.answer: Run terraform plan (with refresh) on a schedule in CI, for example nightly, and alert if it reports any pending changes on production stacks, which signals drift. Terraform Cloud and some tooling offer built-in drift detection. Combined with restricting manual console access, this turns drift from a surprise during your next feature apply into an early, actionable alert, so you can investigate while the context is fresh.

followUps.question: What is terraform import and when do you need it here?
followUps.answer: terraform import brings an existing, unmanaged resource under Terraform's control by writing it into state and mapping it to a resource block you have defined. You need it if the manual change created a brand-new resource (or sub-resource) that Terraform does not track; simply writing the config is not enough because Terraform would try to create a duplicate. Import tells Terraform the resource already exists, after which plan reconciles attributes rather than recreating it.

followUps.question: Why not just let people make console changes when needed?
followUps.answer: Ad-hoc console changes bypass review, leave no audit trail in git, and cause drift that Terraform will later try to undo, potentially at the worst time during an unrelated apply. They also erode the reliability guarantee of IaC, since the code no longer reflects reality. Allowing a controlled break-glass process for genuine emergencies is fine, but it must be paired with promptly codifying the change so the code, state, and reality reconverge.

question: Your Kubernetes CronJob-based pipeline occasionally runs twice for the same schedule, causing duplicate data. How do you diagnose and fix it?
directAnswer: Duplicate runs usually come from overlapping executions or non-idempotent processing. First check the CronJob's concurrencyPolicy, if it is Allow, a slow run can overlap the next scheduled run. Set it to Forbid or Replace to prevent overlap. Then, crucially, make the job itself idempotent so that even a retry or accidental double-run does not duplicate data, using deterministic output paths, upserts/merges, or dedup keys. Also review startingDeadlineSeconds and backoff behavior, which can cause catch-up runs.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: The problem is duplicate side effects from a scheduled batch job. On Kubernetes, CronJobs can overlap runs, retry failed pods, and even fire catch-up executions after downtime, any of which can process the same window twice if the job is not idempotent.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: CronJobs default to concurrencyPolicy Allow, so if a run takes longer than the interval, the next run starts alongside it. Job retries (backoffLimit) rerun a failed pod, and missed schedules can trigger catch-up runs depending on startingDeadlineSeconds. Combined with a job that appends rather than upserts, these produce duplicates.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: You diagnose by inspecting Job and pod history for the CronJob to see whether two Jobs ran for one schedule or a pod retried. You set concurrencyPolicy to Forbid (skip if one is running) or Replace to stop overlap. You bound catch-up behavior with startingDeadlineSeconds. Most importantly you engineer idempotency: write to a deterministic partition keyed by the run's logical date and overwrite it, or use MERGE/upsert with a natural key, so reprocessing the same window yields the same result rather than appending duplicates.

whyImportant: Duplicate data is a serious correctness bug in pipelines, and scheduled jobs are prone to it. The interviewer wants to see both the platform-level fix (concurrency control) and the deeper, more robust fix (idempotency), which is the mark of a mature data engineer who designs for at-least-once execution.
realWorldExample: A nightly aggregation CronJob sometimes overlaps because a heavy run spills past midnight. The team sets concurrencyPolicy to Forbid so the next run is skipped rather than doubling up. They also change the job to overwrite the partition for its logical date rather than appending, so even a manual re-run or a retried pod produces exactly one correct copy of the day's data.

nestedTopics.title: concurrencyPolicy to prevent overlap
nestedTopics.explanation: Forbid skips a new run while the previous is active; Replace kills the old and starts fresh. Either prevents two Jobs from running the same logical work simultaneously, which is the immediate cause of many duplicate-run incidents.

nestedTopics.title: Idempotency as the real fix
nestedTopics.explanation: Concurrency control alone is not enough because retries and catch-up runs still reprocess windows. Designing the job so reprocessing a window is safe, overwrite-by-partition or upsert-by-key, makes correctness independent of how many times it runs.

nestedTopics.title: startingDeadlineSeconds and catch-up
nestedTopics.explanation: If the controller misses schedules (for example during downtime), it may launch catch-up runs. Setting startingDeadlineSeconds bounds how far back it will try to catch up, preventing a flood of belated runs that reprocess old windows.

followUps.question: Why is idempotency more robust than just setting concurrencyPolicy?
followUps.answer: concurrencyPolicy only prevents simultaneous overlap, but duplicates can still arise from retried pods after a transient failure, catch-up runs after downtime, or manual re-runs to fix an issue. All of these reprocess a window that may have already produced output. An idempotent job, one where reprocessing the same logical window overwrites or merges rather than appends, is correct regardless of how many times or when it runs, which is why it is the durable fix rather than a band-aid.

followUps.question: How do you make a job that appends rows idempotent?
followUps.answer: Key the output by a deterministic logical partition, typically the run's data date, and overwrite that partition on each run instead of appending, so re-running replaces rather than adds. Alternatively, use a MERGE/upsert into the target keyed by a natural business key so repeated rows update in place instead of duplicating. A third option is deduplication on write using an idempotency key. The common thread is that the same input window always converges to the same output.

followUps.question: How do you tell whether two Jobs ran or one pod retried?
followUps.answer: Inspect the CronJob's child Jobs and their pods: kubectl get jobs and describing them shows whether two separate Job objects were created for the schedule (an overlap or catch-up) or a single Job had multiple pod attempts (a retry driven by backoffLimit). The distinction points you to the right fix, concurrencyPolicy or startingDeadlineSeconds for multiple Jobs, versus reviewing failure causes and idempotency for retried pods within one Job.

question: A dbt model change that passed CI broke a downstream dashboard in production. How do you improve the pipeline so this cannot happen again?
directAnswer: The gap is that CI validated the change in isolation but did not catch the downstream impact or run against realistic data. Improvements: expand testing to include the downstream models and their data tests (build the changed model plus everything that depends on it), run against representative data in a staging environment that mirrors production, add data contract and schema-change checks, and introduce a staging deployment gate with the actual dashboard queries before promoting to production. Also enforce dbt tests and slim CI (state-based selection) so nothing dependent is skipped.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: This is a CI/CD coverage and environment-parity problem for a data transformation pipeline. The change passed because CI tested only what changed, not its blast radius, and likely used a sample that hid the real breakage.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Data changes have wide, non-local impact: a renamed or retyped column can silently break models and dashboards downstream. If CI does not build and test dependents, or runs on data unlike production, breaking changes slip through even with green checks.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: You strengthen the pipeline in layers. In CI, use dbt's state comparison to select the changed models and their downstream dependents (dbt build --select state:modified+) so dependent models and tests actually run. Add schema/data-contract checks that fail on breaking column changes. Deploy to a staging warehouse that mirrors production data shape, run the full test suite there, and execute the critical dashboard queries as an acceptance check. Only after staging passes do you promote the same artifacts to production, ideally with a manual gate for high-impact changes.

whyImportant: Green CI that still breaks production is a trust-destroying failure mode, and it is common in data because impact is downstream and data-dependent. Designing CI/CD that accounts for lineage, data realism, and environment promotion is exactly what distinguishes a senior data engineer.
realWorldExample: After a dbt model rename broke a revenue dashboard, the team changes CI to run dbt build --select state:modified+ so every downstream model and test runs, and adds a contract test that fails when a column consumed downstream is dropped or retyped. They add a staging step that runs the dashboard's key queries against staging data and gates production promotion on it. The next breaking change is caught in staging, not production.

nestedTopics.title: Test downstream, not just the change
nestedTopics.explanation: Building only the modified model misses its blast radius. Using state:modified+ (the plus selects descendants) runs dependent models and their tests, catching breakages that the isolated change would not reveal.

nestedTopics.title: Environment parity and realistic data
nestedTopics.explanation: Running CI on a tiny or unrepresentative sample can hide issues that only appear at production data shapes. A staging environment that mirrors production structure (and a representative data slice) surfaces breakages before they reach real users.

nestedTopics.title: Data contracts and schema checks
nestedTopics.explanation: Explicit contracts on columns consumed by downstream models or dashboards let CI fail fast when a change violates them (dropping a column, changing a type). This turns silent downstream breakage into an immediate, local CI failure.

followUps.question: What does dbt's state:modified+ selection do and why does it matter here?
followUps.answer: state:modified selects models that changed relative to a stored manifest (the previous production state), and the trailing + extends the selection to include everything downstream of those models. Building and testing that set means CI exercises not just the edited model but all its dependents and their tests, which is exactly where the downstream dashboard breakage would have surfaced. It also keeps CI efficient by skipping unaffected models rather than rebuilding the whole project.

followUps.question: How would a data contract have prevented this?
followUps.answer: A data contract declares the guaranteed shape of a model's output, specific columns, types, and constraints, that downstream consumers depend on. With contracts enforced, a change that drops or retypes a consumed column fails the build immediately with a clear contract violation, rather than silently producing output that breaks a dashboard later. It shifts the failure left, to a local, obvious CI error at the point of change, and makes the interface between producers and consumers explicit and testable.

followUps.question: Why isn't running dbt test on a sample in CI enough?
followUps.answer: A small sample may not contain the data conditions that trigger the failure, nulls, edge values, the specific rows a dashboard aggregates, so tests pass while production data breaks. Sampling also cannot validate downstream query behavior or performance at real scale. That is why you complement CI sample tests with a staging environment that mirrors production data shape and runs the actual downstream queries, catching data-dependent and integration issues that isolated sample tests miss.

question: You need to deploy a new version of a streaming consumer with zero downtime and the ability to roll back instantly if it misbehaves. Which deployment strategy do you choose and how do you implement it?
directAnswer: For instant rollback and zero downtime, a blue-green deployment is the cleanest choice: run the new version (green) alongside the current one (blue), validate green, then switch traffic (or consumer group activation) to green, keeping blue ready to switch back instantly. A canary approach is a good alternative if you want to shift a small fraction first and watch metrics. For a streaming consumer specifically, you must coordinate consumer groups and offsets so you do not double-process or lose messages during the cutover.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: This is a progressive delivery problem for a stateful-ish streaming workload. Blue-green keeps two full environments and flips between them; canary gradually shifts load to the new version while monitoring. Both aim for safe releases without downtime and with fast recovery.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: A rolling update replaces pods in place, which is fine for many services but makes instant rollback harder and can briefly run mixed versions. Blue-green and canary exist to give explicit control over exposure and an immediate escape hatch, which matters when a bad streaming consumer could corrupt or duplicate data.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: In blue-green, you deploy green as a separate Deployment, let it come up and pass health checks, then cut over, for a request service you flip the Service selector; for a consumer you activate green's consumer group and stop blue. Because green was validated before taking traffic, rollback is just switching back to blue. For streaming, you rely on committed offsets and idempotent processing so the cutover does not reprocess or drop events, and you may pause blue only after green is confirmed consuming.

whyImportant: Choosing and correctly implementing a deployment strategy, and understanding the streaming-specific offset and consumer-group nuances, is a strong senior signal. It shows you think about safe releases and data correctness together, not just getting new code running.
realWorldExample: A team deploys a new Kafka enrichment consumer using blue-green: green joins a parallel consumer setup and is validated against a shadow topic and metrics, then they cut the live consumer group over to green and stop blue. Processing is idempotent and offset-committed, so no messages are lost or duplicated at the switch. When a subtle bug appears, they flip back to blue in seconds, restoring the known-good version without a redeploy.

nestedTopics.title: Blue-green for instant rollback
nestedTopics.explanation: Two complete versions coexist; only one is live. Because the standby is fully deployed and validated, switching back is immediate, which is the key advantage when you need to abort a bad release fast. The cost is running double capacity during the transition.

nestedTopics.title: Canary for gradual, metric-driven rollout
nestedTopics.explanation: Canary sends a small percentage to the new version and watches error rates, lag, and latency before ramping up. It limits blast radius and catches problems on a fraction of traffic, at the cost of a slower, more orchestrated rollout.

nestedTopics.title: Streaming-specific offset and group handling
nestedTopics.explanation: For consumers, correctness depends on committed offsets and idempotent processing so a cutover does not reprocess or skip messages. You coordinate consumer groups (or partitions) so exactly the right instances are consuming at any moment during the switch.

followUps.question: What is the main tradeoff of blue-green versus canary?
followUps.answer: Blue-green gives the fastest rollback and a clean all-or-nothing switch, but it requires running two full environments simultaneously (double resources) and exposes 100% of traffic to the new version the instant you cut over, so any issue hits everyone at once. Canary limits blast radius by exposing only a slice first and ramping gradually while watching metrics, but rollback is less instantaneous and the rollout is more complex to orchestrate. Choose blue-green when instant, total rollback matters most; canary when limiting exposure during validation matters most.

followUps.question: Why is idempotency important for a zero-downtime streaming deploy?
followUps.answer: During any cutover there is a window where offsets are committed and consumers hand off, and at-least-once delivery means some messages may be reprocessed. If processing is idempotent, reprocessing produces no duplicate side effects, so the switch is safe even if a few messages cross the boundary twice. Without idempotency, the deploy could double-count or corrupt data at the transition, turning a routine release into a data-quality incident. Idempotency decouples correctness from the exact timing of the handoff.

followUps.question: How would you validate the green version before cutting over?
followUps.answer: Run green in parallel without giving it the live output responsibility: have it consume from a copy or shadow topic, or process alongside blue while writing to a scratch location, and compare its outputs and metrics (throughput, error rate, lag) against blue. You can also run integration and data-quality checks on green's results. Only once green demonstrably matches expected behavior on realistic traffic do you perform the cutover, so the switch carries minimal risk and rollback remains a trivial fallback.

question: Executor pods for your PySpark job on Kubernetes keep getting OOMKilled during a large shuffle, even though the JVM heap looks fine. How do you diagnose and fix it?
directAnswer: OOMKilled means the container exceeded its cgroup memory limit, which includes far more than the JVM heap: off-heap memory, shuffle buffers, and, for PySpark, the Python worker processes. The fix is to size the container memory to account for all of it, raise spark.executor.memoryOverhead (and PySpark worker memory), and reduce per-task memory pressure by increasing partitions so each task handles less data. You verify by checking pod events for OOMKilled and comparing configured overhead against actual usage.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: This is a memory-sizing problem specific to Spark on Kubernetes. The Linux kernel OOM-kills the container when its total memory (heap plus off-heap plus Python plus overhead) exceeds the pod's memory limit, which is why the JVM heap can look healthy while the container still dies.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Spark's memory footprint extends well beyond the JVM heap. Shuffles use off-heap buffers, and PySpark spawns Python worker processes whose memory is not counted in the JVM heap but is counted by the container's cgroup. If the pod memory limit is set only for the heap, a heavy shuffle or large Python payloads push the container over its limit.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: You confirm the cause by describing the pod and seeing the OOMKilled reason, then look at Spark UI memory metrics and executor logs. You increase spark.executor.memoryOverhead (or the fraction) so the container reserves room for off-heap and shuffle, and for PySpark you account for spark.executor.pyspark.memory / Python worker usage. You raise the pod memory request and limit to match total need, and you increase spark.sql.shuffle.partitions so each shuffle partition and task is smaller, lowering peak per-task memory. AQE can also help coalesce and manage skew.

whyImportant: OOMKilled executors are one of the most common and frustrating Spark-on-Kubernetes failures, and the root cause, memory beyond the heap, trips up many engineers. Diagnosing and fixing it correctly demonstrates real operational depth with both Spark internals and Kubernetes resource enforcement.
realWorldExample: A PySpark job's executors die with OOMKilled at 8Gi during a wide join. The heap is set to 6Gi, but the shuffle off-heap buffers plus Python workers push total usage past 8Gi. The team raises spark.executor.memoryOverhead to leave more room, bumps the pod limit to 12Gi, and increases shuffle partitions so each task processes less data. The job then completes without OOMKills.

nestedTopics.title: Container memory > JVM heap
nestedTopics.explanation: The pod's memory limit governs total container memory: JVM heap, off-heap, shuffle buffers, and Python workers. A healthy heap does not prevent OOMKill if these other consumers push the container total over the limit; you must size for the sum, not just the heap.

nestedTopics.title: spark.executor.memoryOverhead
nestedTopics.explanation: This config reserves memory for non-heap needs (off-heap, shuffle, and container overhead). Under-setting it is a classic cause of OOMKilled executors on Kubernetes; raising it gives the container headroom for shuffle-heavy or PySpark workloads.

nestedTopics.title: Reduce per-task memory via partitions
nestedTopics.explanation: More shuffle partitions mean smaller partitions and less data per task, lowering peak memory. Increasing spark.sql.shuffle.partitions (and enabling AQE for skew) spreads the shuffle so no single task blows the memory budget.

followUps.question: How do you confirm the failure was OOMKilled versus another crash?
followUps.answer: Run kubectl describe pod on the failed executor and look at the container's last state and reason; OOMKilled appears there explicitly, along with the exit code (137). You can corroborate with node-level memory metrics and the Spark UI/executor logs showing memory pressure near the failure. Distinguishing OOMKilled from other exits matters because the remedy, more memory headroom and smaller partitions, is specific to running out of container memory, not to, say, a code exception or a lost node.

followUps.question: Why does PySpark specifically increase OOMKill risk?
followUps.answer: PySpark runs Python worker processes separate from the JVM to execute Python UDFs and serialize data between the JVM and Python. That Python memory lives outside the JVM heap but still counts against the container's cgroup limit, so heavy Python payloads or many workers can push the container over its limit even when the heap is fine. You account for it by budgeting spark.executor.pyspark.memory / overhead and, where possible, preferring built-in Spark functions over Python UDFs to reduce cross-boundary memory pressure.

followUps.question: Would simply increasing the memory limit always fix it?
followUps.answer: Raising the limit can resolve immediate OOMKills, but it is not always the best or sufficient fix: it costs more per pod, packs fewer pods per node, and does not address root causes like data skew, where one task gets a giant partition and would blow any reasonable limit. Combining a sensible memory increase with more partitions, adequate overhead, and skew handling (AQE, salting) is more robust and cost-effective than throwing memory at a skewed or oversized-task problem.
